messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malcolm sat at the edge of his desk when the pain arrived, a sudden, crushing weight that dropped him onto the polished floor of his office. Paramedics found him unresponsive and rushed him to the intensive care unit, where they intubated him and administered paralytics to keep his lungs moving while his heart stuttered through dangerous arrhythmias. For four days, Malcolm remained conscious but completely immobilized, watching the clinical staff adjust his settings while machines regulated his breathing. He understood he was dying, and the terror of being locked inside a failing body, unable to command his own chest, left a permanent imprint. When the sedation finally lifted and he was moved to a step-down ward, the immediate panic subsided, but the physical aftermath did not. The tension settled into his shoulders and jaw, never fully releasing. Malcolm found himself checking the deadbolts on his front door and the windows in his study long after they were secured, certain that if he stopped monitoring the perimeter, he would be caught off guard. His body remained constantly tense, braced as if expecting another sudden collapse. At work, the difficulty concentrating made his role untenable. He sat before stacks of legislative drafts and budget projections, but his eyes would slide across the text without taking hold. He would reread the same paragraph repeatedly, losing the thread of the argument, his attention fracturing whenever a colleague’s pen clicked in a steady rhythm. The sound pulled him back to the ICU ventilator’s metronome pace; he would have to stop his work, press his palms flat against the desk, and wait until his breathing settled. He began leaving the policy analysis wing an hour early, telling his supervisor he was managing fatigue, though the truth was that the fluorescent lights and the hum of office equipment felt like a countdown to another crisis. The memories of the hospital did not arrive as quiet reflections. Sometimes they slid over him with a chilling flatness; he could describe the sterile air, the taste of the breathing tube, the weight of the paralytic, but he felt completely numb, as if recalling a stranger’s nightmare. Other times, the past refused to stay in the past. He would be unlocking his car and suddenly the ground beneath him felt like the hospital mattress, the blanket pressing down, his lungs burning for air he could not draw. He had to stop mid-stride, gripping the door handle until his knuckles turned white, until the present rushed back. When the emotion finally broke through, it was overwhelming; he would sit in his living room, hands shaking, and force himself to close his eyes and breathe, knowing that pushing through only left him hollow. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the quiet satisfaction of a finished report or the comfort of a morning coffee belonged to a man who no longer existed. What frightened him most was his own physiology. He watched his pulse in the morning light, counting beats, measuring breaths, certain that his body kept reacting as if he were still in the ICU long after he was safe. He could no longer trust his own body to keep him upright, to regulate his breathing, to simply carry him through a day without warning of another failure. Over the months, the avoidance habits hardened into routine. Malcolm stopped chairing the annual policy review, delegating his sections to junior analysts and citing vague health appointments. He avoided gyms, then grocery stores, then the community center where his late wife had volunteered, because crowded spaces made his chest tighten and his shoulders knot. He began scheduling every errand for early Tuesday mornings, when the parking lots were empty and the roads quiet. Now, at sixty-eight, he sat in the waiting room of a community mental health clinic, his hands folded tightly over his knees. He had come because his daughter finally insisted he stop managing alone, because the silence in his house had grown too heavy, and because he could no longer ignore the way his days were shrinking. He hoped someone might help him quiet the constant scan of the room, might help him understand why his own chest felt like a locked space, and might help him remember how to live without waiting for the next alarm.
